title: Nabta Playa: The Stones That Watched the Sky
claim: Was Nabta Playa's stone circle an astronomical observatory, 7,000 years ago?

lines: [d:intrigue][sfx:boom][act:hushed, wonder]About seven thousand years ago, in the Egyptian Sahara, cattle herders set up a small circle of ^stones.
[d:tension][act:the question, leaning in][tune:rise]Was it the world's first ^observatory? [act:explaining, plain]A place built to watch the ^sky?

[go:1|1.43][d:calm][act:plain, orienting]The place is called Nabta ^Playa. [act:steady, factual]It lies about a hundred kilometres west of Abu ^Simbel, in the far south of ^Egypt. [p:0.93][act:explaining, a simple picture]A playa is a dry lake bed: a flat hollow that only holds water after ^rain. [act:steady, vivid]Back then, summer rains filled it into a seasonal ^lake, and herders came with their ^cattle.

[go:2|1.6][d:build][act:building, precise]The circle is small: only about four metres ^across. [act:light, a small smile]You could cross it in five ^strides. [act:pointing them out]Around its edge stand four pairs of upright ^stones, like little ^gateposts. [p:0.93][act:the claim, intrigued]Look through two of the gaps, and your line of sight runs north to ^south. [act:the second one, wonder]And a second line points to where the sun rises at ^midsummer, on the longest day of the ^year.

[go:3|1.43][d:build][act:the reveal, strong]It dates to about {4800|forty-eight hundred} BCE. [p:0.93][act:context, wonder]That's some eighteen centuries before the first phase of ^Stonehenge. [act:a picture of time, unhurried]Eighteen centuries: about as long as the time that separates ^us from the Roman ^Empire.

[d:build][go:4|1.64][act:vivid]Nearby, cattle were buried in clay-lined ^chambers. [p:0.93][act:vivid, impressed]And stones nearly three metres ^tall, taller than the ceiling of a room, were dragged across the sand into ^lines.

[go:5|1.43][d:reveal][act:fair, the challenger's case]Some go much ^further. [act:presenting it, fair]They see lines to bright ^stars, even a map of the constellation ^Orion, laid out in stone. [p:0.93][act:explaining, clear]But the stars shift slowly over the centuries, so a line to a star only works at one ^time. [p:0.9][act:the reply, precise]And those star dates fall about fifteen hundred years ^before the stones were set up. [act:fair, careful]Some stones may also have ^moved since.
[d:build][act:plain, a small smile][tune:fall]Even the excavators say its nickname, the calendar circle, may be the wrong ^name.

[go:6|2.23][d:verdict][p:0.95][act:weighing it, even][tune:rise]The world's first ^observatory? [act:the verdict, measured][tune:fall]*Mixed ^record@noun*. [act:fair]A real ritual landscape, probably watching the ^sun. [act:fair, explaining]The north line and the midsummer sunrise hold up ^well.
[d:tension][p:0.93][act:the last word, warm][tune:fall]The star maps are a ^stretch.

post: A small stone circle in the Egyptian Sahara, about 7,000 years old, with gaps facing north and the midsummer sunrise. What it probably was, and where the observatory claims overreach.
sources: Malville et al. 1998 (doi:10.1038/33131) · Wendorf & Schild 1998 (doi:10.1006/jaar.1998.0319) · Wendorf & Malville 2001 (doi:10.1007/978-1-4615-0653-9) · Malville 2015 (doi:10.1007/978-1-4614-6141-8_101) · Brophy & Rosen 2005 · Belmonte 2010 (ICOMOS/IAU)

title: Tutankhamun's Sky-Glass
claim: Is the scarab on Tutankhamun's pectoral made of glass melted by a cosmic impact?
hook_text: A scarab made by a *cosmic* blast.

lines: [d:intrigue][sfx:boom][act:hushed, intrigued]In a jewel worn on the chest of the pharaoh ^Tutankhamun sits a yellow-green ^scarab, a sacred beetle of ancient ^Egypt.
[d:tension][act:the twist, leaning in][tune:fall]It isn't a ^gemstone. [act:the reveal, slow][tune:fall]It's ^glass, melted by something from ^space.

[go:1|1.42][d:calm][act:plain, orienting]That glass comes from the Great Sand ^Sea, an ocean of dunes near the border of Egypt and ^Libya. [act:vivid]There, pieces of it lie scattered on the ^sand, like the shards of a giant broken ^bottle.

[d:build][go:2|1.69][act:steady, precise]It is almost pure ^silica, the same stuff as sand and window ^glass. [p:0.9][act:the big number]And it is about twenty-nine million years ^old. [p:0.93][act:curious, the method]How do we ^know? [act:explaining, clear]A few uranium atoms inside the glass split, now and then, and each one leaves a tiny scar, a ^track. [act:explaining, a simple picture]Count the tracks, like tally marks, and you can read@present the ^age. [act:light, a small smile]Much later, Stone Age people made ^tools from it.

[go:3|1.75][d:build][act:storytelling]In {1922|nineteen twenty-two}, Howard ^Carter, the man who found Tutankhamun's tomb, listed the scarab as ^chalcedony, a common ^stone. [p:0.93][act:storytelling, building]Some seventy years later, in the {1990s|nineteen nineties}, a mineralogist, an expert in minerals, looked ^again. [act:the reveal, delighted]It was desert@noun ^glass.

[go:4|1.43][d:build][act:building, curious]So what melted ^it? [p:0.93][act:explaining, clear]Tiny crystals in the glass keep traces of a mineral that forms only in ^impacts, under the crushing shock of a rock from space hitting at enormous ^speed. [act:explaining, plain]No volcano can squeeze that ^hard. [p:0.9][act:vivid]And the melt passed two thousand seven hundred and fifty ^degrees Celsius: more than twice as hot as ^lava.

[go:5|1.74][d:reveal][act:the crux, curious][tune:fall]But where's the ^crater? [act:explaining, plain]An impact usually leaves a ^hole, and here, none has been ^confirmed. [act:fair, the challenger's case]So some argue for an ^airburst: a rock from space that explodes high in the ^sky. [p:0.93][act:explaining, vivid]Its blast of heat melts the sand below, without leaving a ^hole.
[go:6|0.8][d:build][act:plain]One candidate crater, ^Kebira, was put to the ^test. [act:plain, a small shrug][tune:fall]It ^failed.

[go:7|1.65][d:verdict][p:0.95][act:weighing it, calm][tune:rise]A pharaoh's jewel made by a cosmic ^impact? [act:the verdict, measured][tune:fall]*Strong ^evidence*. [act:fair, sorting it out]A crater, or a blast in the air: either way, the evidence points to ^space.
[d:tension][p:0.93][act:the last word, a small smile][tune:fall]The crater is still ^missing.

post: The yellow-green scarab on Tutankhamun's pectoral is Libyan Desert Glass, melted about 29 million years ago by a cosmic impact or airburst. What the glass shows, and the crater nobody has found.
sources: Cavosie & Koeberl 2019 (doi:10.1130/G45974.1) · Kovaleva et al. 2019 (doi:10.1111/maps.13250) · Kovaleva & Helmy 2023 (doi:10.2138/am-2022-8759) · Boslough & Crawford 2008 (doi:10.1016/j.ijimpeng.2008.07.053) · de Michele 1998

title: The Ghost Lineage of the Green Sahara
claim: Do the first Green Sahara genomes reveal a North African lineage that stayed apart for tens of thousands of years?

lines: [d:intrigue][sfx:boom][act:hushed, tender]About seven thousand years ago, in a Sahara that was ^green, two women were laid to rest in a rock ^shelter.
[d:tension][act:the reveal, leaning in][tune:fall]Their DNA belongs to a human ^lineage, a family line, that no one ^knew.

[go:1|1.43][d:calm][act:plain, orienting]The shelter is called ^Takarkori, in the mountains of south-west ^Libya. [act:steady]Today, all around it is ^desert@noun. [p:0.93][act:painting it, warm]But back then, herders lived here with their ^cattle, beside lakes and ^grassland.

[go:2|1.3][d:build][act:gentle, careful]After death, the dry desert@noun air preserved the two women ^naturally. [act:gentle, explaining]Their bodies dried before they could decay: natural ^mummies, with no embalming at ^all.

[go:3|1.65][d:build][act:the reveal, precise]In {2025|twenty twenty-five}, scientists read@past their ^genomes, the full instruction book written in our ^DNA. [p:0.93][act:explaining, a simple picture]Each time DNA is passed down the generations, a few tiny typos creep ^in. [act:explaining, clear]Two family lines that split long ago pile up different ^typos: count them, and you can tell how long they've been ^apart. [p:0.9][act:building, amazed]Their line split from other African lineages about fifty thousand years ^ago. [act:the twist, wonder][tune:fall]And then it stayed ^apart.
[d:build][go:4|1.44][act:connecting it, curious][tune:rise]Their closest known ^relatives? [act:the payoff, delighted]People who lived in ^Morocco, fifteen thousand years ^earlier.

[go:5|1.67][d:build][act:the point, clear]So the green Sahara's herders were mostly ^local. [p:0.93][act:thoughtful]Cattle and milk arrived as ^ideas, passed from neighbour to neighbour, not with a wave of ^newcomers. [act:light, a small smile]And their pots hold Africa's earliest known milk ^fats. [p:0.93][act:explaining, the method]Fat soaks into bare clay, like oil into a wooden chopping ^board, and chemists can still detect it, thousands of years ^later.

[go:6|1.43][d:reveal][act:fair, a caveat]But two people from one site are not a whole ^people. [p:0.93][act:explaining, a simple picture]It's like describing a whole town from just two of its ^residents. [act:precise]Teeth and culture found elsewhere hint at more ^movement: people coming, and ^going.

[go:7|2.25][d:verdict][p:0.95][act:weighing it, even][tune:rise]A lost lineage in the green ^Sahara? [act:the verdict, measured][tune:fall]*Strong ^evidence*. [act:fair]For these two women, the result is ^clear. [act:fair, a caveat]How far it reaches is ^not.
[d:tension][p:0.93][act:the last word, inviting][tune:fall]Now we need more ^genomes.

post: Two women who died in a green Sahara about 7,000 years ago carry a North African lineage that split off some 50,000 years ago. What their genomes say about the herders, and what two people can't tell us.
sources: Salem, van de Loosdrecht et al. 2025 (doi:10.1038/s41586-025-08793-7) · Dunne et al. 2012 (doi:10.1038/nature11186) · Di Vincenzo et al. 2015

title: Tassili: The Great Martian God
claim: Do the Round Head paintings of Tassili n'Ajjer show ancient astronauts?

lines: [d:intrigue][sfx:boom][act:playful, intrigued]In the {1950s|nineteen fifties}, an explorer stood before a painted giant in the Sahara, up to five metres ^tall, and nicknamed it the great Martian ^god.
[d:tension][act:dry, a small smile][tune:fall]It was a ^joke. [act:dry][tune:fall]Some people took him ^literally.

[go:1|1.44][d:calm][act:plain, orienting]The place is Tassili ^n'Ajjer, a sandstone plateau in south-east ^Algeria, riddled with rock ^shelters. [act:warm, vivid]For thousands of years, people painted on their ^walls.

[d:build][go:2|1.7][act:quietly amazed]It holds more than fifteen thousand ancient ^images, painted and ^engraved. [p:0.93][act:playful, doing the sum]Look at one a minute@time, eight hours a day, and you'd need about a ^month to see them all.

[go:3|1.75][d:build][act:presenting it, fair]One early style is called the Round ^Heads. [act:presenting it, vivid]Their heads are smooth ^circles: no eyes, no nose, no ^mouth. [act:the challenger's case, fair]By {1968|nineteen sixty-eight}, writers about ancient astronauts saw space ^helmets. [act:plain, fair]And to be fair, they really are unlike the art that came ^later.

[go:4|1.66][d:build][act:grave, measured]But the real damage came from the ^copyists. [p:0.93][act:precise]To make the colours stand out for their copies, the team wetted the paintings and sponged ^them. [act:grave][tune:fall]The colours brightened for a ^moment, and then faded ^faster.
[d:build][act:the sting, quiet][tune:fall]And some of the published pictures were later said to be ^fakes.

[go:5|1.75][d:reveal][act:fair, clear]So what are the Round ^Heads? [p:0.93][act:explaining, the method]Paint is hard to date directly, so archaeologists date them ^indirectly: from the layers around them, and from which images were painted over which, like posters pasted over older ^posters. [p:0.9][act:precise]The answer: about nine and a half to seven and a half thousand years ^ago. [act:thoughtful]The blank heads look like a ^convention, a way of painting: masks, body paint, or spirit ^beings.
[d:build][act:respectful, even]And Tuareg tradition credits some of the paintings to ^spirits. [act:respectful, warm][tune:fall]A living ^belief.

[go:6|2.25][d:verdict][p:0.95][act:weighing it, calm][tune:rise]Astronauts on the ^rocks? [act:the verdict, firm][tune:fall]*Ruled ^out*. [act:fair, explaining]A smooth head is a painting ^style, not a ^helmet. [act:warm, the other half]And the art is extraordinary on its ^own.
[d:tension][p:0.93][act:the last word, quiet][tune:fall]It deserves better ^copies.

post: A 1950s explorer joked that a giant painted figure in the Sahara was the 'great Martian god', and ancient-astronaut writers took him at his word. What the Round Heads are, and the real scandal of how they were copied.

title: The Day the Sahara Switched Off
claim: Did the Green Sahara end abruptly, within a few generations?

lines: [d:intrigue][sfx:boom][act:hushed, wonder]Where the Sahara is now, there was once a lake about the size of the Caspian ^Sea, the biggest lake on Earth ^today.
[d:tension][act:the question, leaning in]Then the rain ^stopped. [act:curious][tune:rise]Fast, or ^slow?

[go:1|1.41][d:calm][act:plain, explaining]From about eleven thousand to five thousand years ago, the Sahara was ^green. [act:vivid]Monsoon rains, summer rains blowing in from the ^ocean, reached deep into the ^desert@noun, and filled its ^lakes.

[d:build][go:2|1.68][act:curious, the method][tune:rise]^Why? [p:0.93][act:explaining, clear]A slow wobble in Earth's orbit, over thousands of years, gave northern summers a little more ^sunshine. [act:explaining, a simple picture]Warm land heats the air above it, the air rises, and wet ocean air flows in to take its ^place. [p:0.9][act:vivid]At its height, rain fell at about ten times today's ^rate.

[go:3|1.43][d:build][act:curious, the method]So how do we know when the rain ^stopped? [p:0.93][act:explaining, a simple picture]Mud and dust settle layer by layer at the bottom of lakes and ^seas, like the pages of a ^diary. [act:explaining, clear]Scientists drill out a tube of it, a sediment ^core, and read@present it page by ^page. [act:building, precise]Off the coast of ^Mauritania, the dust blown out from the land jumps about five and a half thousand years ago, within decades to ^centuries. [p:0.93][act:the counterpoint]But a lake in Chad records@verb a slow change, over thousands of ^years.

[go:4|1.65][d:build][act:grave, measured]Lake Mega-Chad shrank fast, about five thousand years ^ago. [act:the twist, wonder]Its last basin, the ^Bodélé, held water until only about a thousand years ^ago. [act:vivid]Now it's bone dry, and it is Earth's biggest source of ^dust.

[go:5|1.42][d:reveal][act:fair, weighing][tune:rise]So, was it a ^collapse? [act:clear]The best answer: sudden in some places, gradual in ^others. [act:dry, light][tune:rise]A single catastrophe that ended it ^all? [act:dry, firm][tune:fall]No evidence at ^all.
[go:6|1.3][d:build][act:curious, even]And ^people? [act:fair, even]Some argue that herders and their grazing cattle sped up the ^end. [act:the counterpoint, curious]One model says they ^slowed it.

[go:7|1.3][d:verdict][p:0.95][act:weighing it, even][tune:rise]The Sahara switched off ^overnight? [act:the verdict, measured][tune:fall]*Mixed ^record@noun*. [act:fair]The green Sahara itself is well ^established.
[d:tension][p:0.93][act:the last word, warm][tune:fall]How fast it faded depends on where you ^stand.

post: A lake the size of the Caspian Sea once filled the southern Sahara. Then the monsoon weakened. Did the green Sahara collapse in a few generations, or fade over thousands of years?

title: The Embrace at Gobero
claim: Were Gobero's two phases of burials made by two different peoples, or one?

lines: [d:intrigue][sfx:boom][act:hushed, tender]About five thousand three hundred years ago, in what is now the Sahara ^desert@noun, a woman and two children were buried together, in an ^embrace.
[d:tension][act:quiet, wonder][tune:fall]On a bed of ^flowers.

[go:1|1.44][d:calm][act:plain, orienting]The place is ^Gobero, in ^Niger, today a sea of sand on the southern edge of the ^Sahara. [act:storytelling]In {2000|two thousand}, a team led by Paul ^Sereno found a cemetery there, beside a lake that has since ^vanished.

[d:build][go:2|1.68][act:impressed]About two hundred ^burials. [p:0.93][act:vivid]And around them, the bones of fish, ^hippos and ^crocodiles. [act:explaining, clear]Hippos and crocodiles need deep water all year ^round. [act:explaining, plain][tune:fall]So this was a real ^lake, up to about three kilometres ^wide.

[go:3|1.77][d:build][act:building, precise]The first people buried here are called the ^Kiffian. [act:vivid]From about {7700|seventy-seven hundred} BCE, they fished the lake with ^harpoons. [act:grave]Then came a long dry spell, and the lake ^emptied. [p:0.93][act:grave, quiet][tune:fall]For about a thousand years, no one was buried ^here.
[d:build][act:the change]When the water came back, so did the ^burials. [act:the change, precise]But they looked ^different. [act:steady]These people are called the ^Tenerians, and they kept ^cattle.

[go:4|1.69][d:build][act:tender, careful]The embrace belongs to this second, Tenerian ^phase. [p:0.93][act:gentle, explaining]Pollen grains are tiny and tough, and each kind of plant has its own ^shape, like a ^signature. [act:gentle][tune:fall]Here, pollen suggests that flowers were laid in the ^grave.

[go:5|1.75][d:reveal][act:fair, even]In {2008|two thousand eight}, the team saw two different ^peoples, a thousand years ^apart. [p:0.93][act:curious, the method]But how can you tell who is ^related? [act:explaining, a simple picture]One clue is ^teeth: their little bumps and grooves run in families, a bit like the shape of a ^nose. [act:the twist, precise]In {2025|twenty twenty-five}, a study of their teeth, with Sereno as a co-author, found the two groups hard to tell ^apart.

[go:6|2.25][d:verdict][p:0.95][act:weighing it, even][tune:rise]One people, or ^two? [act:the verdict, measured][tune:fall]*Open ^question*. [act:fair]Ancient DNA could ^settle it, if any survives the desert@noun ^heat.
[d:tension][p:0.93][act:the last word, warm, gentle][tune:fall]Either way, someone loved ^them.

post: A lakeside cemetery in today's Ténéré desert, used for thousands of years, and a woman and two children buried together on flowers. Two peoples, or one? The teeth have changed the answer.
sources: Sereno et al. 2008 (doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0002995) · Stojanowski, Irish & Sereno 2025 (doi:10.1002/ajpa.70262) · Stojanowski & Knudson 2011 (doi:10.1002/ajpa.21542)

title: Swimmers in the Sand
claim: Do the painted 'swimmers' of Wadi Sura show real swimming, or the dead in a watery afterworld?

lines: [d:intrigue][sfx:boom][act:hushed, intrigued]Someone painted ^swimmers, in one of the driest places on ^Earth, where it hardly ever ^rains. [act:vivid, quiet]Little red figures, arms and legs spread wide.
[d:tension][act:the question, leaning in][tune:rise]Were they swimming, or ^dead?

[go:1|1.41][d:calm][act:storytelling]In {1933|nineteen thirty-three}, the explorer ^Almásy found this cave, in the far south-west of ^Egypt. [act:steady]He called it the Cave of ^Swimmers. [act:light, a small smile]Decades later, the film The English ^Patient made it ^famous.

[go:2|1.69][d:build][act:impressed, building]In {2002|two thousand two}, a second shelter turned up ^nearby: the Cave of ^Beasts. [p:0.93][act:vivid, painting it]Its painted wall is seventeen metres ^wide, as long as ten people lying head to ^toe. [p:0.9][act:impressed]And on it, five to eight thousand ^figures. [act:vivid, listing them][tune:fall]Hands, ^swimmers, and headless ^beasts.

[d:build][go:3|1.43][act:explaining, a simple picture]Some of the hands are ^stencils: press something to the rock, blow paint around it, and its outline ^stays. [act:curious, setting it up]A few tiny ones looked like a baby's ^hands. [act:delighted, a little amazed]A closer look showed they were made with the feet of ^lizards.

[go:4|1.74][d:build][act:fair, even]So what do the swimmers ^mean? [act:fair, the first reading]Almásy thought they showed a real ^lake, from a time when this desert@noun was ^green. [act:the other reading, measured]Many archaeologists see something ^else: the dead, floating in the dark waters that came before ^creation. [p:0.93][act:explaining, careful]In later Egyptian belief, the world rose out of a dark, endless ^ocean. [act:explaining, careful]And that idea, with the dead drifting in those waters, appears in Egyptian ^tombs.

[go:5|1.43][d:reveal][act:the crux, precise]The paintings date to roughly six and a half to four and a half thousand years ^BCE. [act:fair]The Egyptian texts come two or three thousand years ^later. [p:0.93][act:a picture of time, unhurried]That's like explaining a Roman mosaic with a book written ^today. [p:0.93][act:explaining, fair]Ideas can travel that far in time, but they ^change on the way. [act:plain][tune:fall]A long gap to ^bridge.

[go:6|2.21][d:verdict][p:0.95][act:weighing it, even][tune:rise]Did Egyptian ideas of the afterlife begin in these ^caves? [act:the verdict, measured][tune:fall]*Open ^question*. [act:fair]Possible, but the bridge across all those centuries is still ^missing.
[d:tension][p:0.93][act:the last word, warm, a small smile][tune:fall]The swimmers aren't telling ^yet.

post: Painted swimmers in one of the driest places on Earth, and a second cave with thousands of figures and hand stencils made with lizard feet. Real swimmers, or the dead in the waters before creation?
sources: Kuper (ed.) 2013, Wadi Sura: The Cave of Beasts · Honoré et al. 2016 (doi:10.1016/j.jasrep.2016.02.014) · di Lernia & Gallinaro 2010 (doi:10.1017/S0003598X00067016) · Förster, Riemer & Kuper 2012

title: The Kingdom That Drank Its Fossil Water
claim: Did the Garamantes' desert state fade when its ancient groundwater ran out?

lines: [d:intrigue][sfx:boom][act:intrigued, measured]Rome called them ^barbarians. [act:the reveal, leaning in]Yet they built towns, pyramids, and hundreds of kilometres of underground ^tunnels, dug by ^hand.
[d:tension][act:the twist][tune:fall]In the middle of the ^Sahara.

[go:1|1.43][d:calm][act:plain, orienting]They are the ^Garamantes, of Fezzan, in south-west ^Libya. [p:0.93][act:steady]Their kingdom lasted from about a thousand BCE to seven hundred ^CE: some seventeen ^centuries. [act:amused, storytelling]The Greek historian ^Herodotus describes their ^chariots. [act:amused, the punchline]And cattle that grazed walking ^backwards, because their horns curved so far ^forward.

[go:2|1.66][d:build][act:building, precise]Their secret was ^water. [act:vivid]They dug underground canals, called ^foggaras, to tap ancient ^groundwater. [p:0.93][act:explaining, clear]Each canal slopes gently down, under the ground, from the water out to the fields and palm ^groves, so the water flows on its own, with no ^pumps. [act:explaining, plain]Along the way, shafts from the surface let the diggers in, and let air ^down. [p:0.9][act:vivid, precise]On average, those shafts are about nine metres ^deep: as deep as a three-storey house@noun is ^tall.

[go:3|1.43][d:build][act:impressed]With that water came oasis ^towns, the first in the ^Sahara. [p:0.93][act:vivid, precise]And small pyramid ^tombs, built of mud brick, three to four and a half metres ^tall. [act:plain]And trade across the desert@noun kept them ^rich, as goods passed through their oases from one side of the Sahara to the ^other.

[go:4|1.43][d:reveal][act:grave, measured]But that groundwater fell as rain thousands of years earlier, in wetter ^times. [p:0.93][act:explaining, a simple picture]It's fossil water: like a savings account that gets no new ^deposits. [act:grave][tune:fall]What you draw out doesn't come ^back. [act:precise]As the water table sank, the canals ran dry, one by ^one.

[go:5|0.8][d:build][act:fair, careful]Other things played a part ^too. [act:fair, even][tune:level]Shifting ^trade. [act:fair, careful][tune:fall]And fewer workers to dig and clean the canals: workers who were perhaps ^enslaved.

[go:6|1.72][d:verdict][p:0.95][act:weighing it, even][tune:rise]A desert@noun kingdom that drank its fossil ^water? [act:the verdict, measured][tune:fall]^*Plausible*. [act:fair]A leading explanation, but not the only ^one.
[d:tension][p:0.93][act:the last word, quiet][tune:fall]A warning, perhaps, written in ^tunnels.

post: The Garamantes built the Sahara's first towns, pyramid tombs and hundreds of kilometres of underground canals, all on ancient groundwater. Did the water running out bring them down?
sources: Mattingly & Sterry 2013 (doi:10.1017/S0003598X00049097) · Wilson 2012 (doi:10.1080/0067270X.2012.727614) · Sterry, Mattingly & Wilson 2022 · Sterry & Mattingly (eds) 2020 · Herodotus 4.183

title: When the Sahara Was Green · The Ledger
claim: What held up, and what didn't, across the Sahara.

lines: [d:intrigue][sfx:boom][p:0.94][act:hushed, drawing us in]Imagine the ^Sahara, but ^green, with a lake about the size of the Caspian ^Sea. [go:1|1.3][act:the big question, clear][tune:rise]So what does@verb the sand still ^remember? [act:bright, rolling up sleeves][tune:fall]Let's investigate ^eight cases, one by ^one.

[d:calm][gap:0.4][go:2|1.5][p:0.93][act:storytelling, like a guide]First stop: the green ^Sahara, from about eleven to five thousand years ^ago. [go:3|.6][act:the question, leaning in][tune:rise]When the rains failed, did it switch off ^overnight? [go:4|.6][act:explaining]Ocean dust off Mauritania jumps within ^centuries. [act:the counterpoint]But a lake in Chad records@verb a slow change, over ^thousands of years. [go:5|.6][act:the verdict, measured][tune:fall]Switched off overnight: *mixed ^record@noun*. [act:fair, warm]The green Sahara itself is well ^established.

[gap:0.4][go:6|1.5][p:0.93][act:storytelling, intrigued]On Tutankhamun's chest sits a yellow-green ^scarab, made of desert@noun ^glass. [go:7|.6][act:the claim, wide-eyed][tune:rise]Glass melted by something from ^space? [go:8|.6][p:0.9][act:explaining, building]Tiny crystals in it hold traces of a mineral made only in ^impacts: a fingerprint at the ^scene. [act:the catch, curious]But the crater is still ^missing. [go:9|.6][act:the verdict, measured][tune:fall]A jewel made by a cosmic impact: *strong ^evidence*.

[d:build][gap:0.4][go:10|1.5][p:0.93][act:tender, storytelling]Two women who died about seven thousand years ago, in a green ^Sahara. [go:11|.6][act:the question][tune:rise]Were its herders ^newcomers? [go:12|.6][p:0.9][act:explaining]Their DNA: a branch of the human family ^tree that split off some fifty thousand years ago, and stayed ^apart. [act:the point, clear]So the herders were mostly ^local. [go:13|.6][act:the verdict, measured][tune:fall]A lost lineage: *strong ^evidence*. [act:fair]But two people aren't a whole ^people.

[gap:0.4][go:14|1.5][p:0.93][act:storytelling, intrigued]The ^Garamantes: oasis towns, pyramid ^tombs, and hundreds of kilometres of ^tunnels. [go:15|.6][act:the question][tune:rise]Why did their kingdom ^fade? [go:16|.6][act:explaining, grave]Their tunnels tapped water that fell as rain in wetter ^times, and it doesn't come ^back. [p:0.9][act:the everyday picture]Like savings with no ^income: one day, they're ^gone. [go:17|.6][act:the verdict, measured][tune:fall]*^Plausible*: a leading explanation, not the only ^one.

[d:build][gap:0.4][go:18|1.5][p:0.93][act:storytelling]^Nabta Playa, in Egypt: a stone circle only four metres across, from about {4800|forty-eight hundred} ^BCE. [go:19|.6][act:the claim][tune:rise]The world's first ^observatory, mapping the ^stars? [go:20|.6][act:explaining, precise]Two gaps line up north to ^south; another faces the midsummer ^sunrise. [act:the catch]But the star dates fall some fifteen hundred years before the ^stones. [go:21|.6][act:the verdict, measured][tune:fall]*Mixed ^record@noun*: the ^sun, probably; the stars, a ^stretch.

[gap:0.4][go:22|1.5][p:0.93][act:tender, hushed]In ^Niger, by a vanished lake: a woman and two children, buried in an ^embrace. [go:23|.6][act:the question][tune:rise]Two phases of burials: two different ^peoples? [go:24|.6][act:explaining]In {2008|two thousand eight}, the team thought ^so. [act:the twist, precise]In {2025|twenty twenty-five}, a study of their teeth found them hard to tell ^apart. [go:25|.6][act:the verdict, measured][tune:fall]*Open ^question*. [act:fair]Ancient DNA could settle ^it.

[d:build][gap:0.4][go:26|1.5][p:0.93][act:storytelling, intrigued]In one of the driest places on ^Earth, someone painted ^swimmers. [go:27|.6][act:the question, fair][tune:rise]A real ^lake, or the dead, in the waters before ^creation, as in later Egyptian ^tombs? [go:28|.6][act:the catch, precise]The paintings are two or three thousand years older than those tomb ^texts. [p:0.9][act:the everyday picture]Like explaining a Roman mosaic with a guidebook written ^today. [go:29|.6][act:the verdict, measured][tune:fall]*Open ^question*. [act:a small smile]The swimmers aren't telling ^yet.

[gap:0.4][go:30|1.5][p:0.93][act:storytelling, playful]Last stop: ^Tassili, in Algeria, and a painted giant nicknamed the great Martian ^god. [go:31|.6][act:the claim, fair]Its round head is smooth and ^featureless. [act:the question][tune:rise]A ^helmet? [go:32|.6][act:explaining]Blank heads look like a ^convention: masks, body paint, or spirit ^beings. [act:grave, measured]The real scandal? [act:grave]Copyists wetted the paintings to brighten ^them, and they faded ^faster. [go:33|.6][act:the verdict, firm][tune:fall]Astronauts on the rocks: *ruled ^out*.

[d:verdict][gap:0.5][go:34|2][p:0.93][act:stepping back, calm]So what do our eight cases say ^together? [go:35|.8][act:clear, warm]The Sahara isn't an empty space on the ^map. [go:36|.8][act:wonder]It's an ^archive of rain, genes, glass and ^paint, drying in the ^sun. [go:37|.8][act:tender, sincere][tune:fall]And its oldest stories are ^human ones: people who herded, painted, and loved their ^dead.
[d:tension][p:0.93][go:38|4][act:the motto, quiet and sure][tune:fall]^Coherence is the measure. [gap:0.45][act:gentle, the closing note][tune:fall]Not ^final demonstration.

post: The verdicts of When the Sahara Was Green in one ledger: what is established about the green Sahara, what is plausible or mixed, what is still open, and what is ruled out.
